Residents without regular internet access may be underrepresented.

content.heading: Produce and audit a compact summary
content.text: Write 70–90 words summarizing the practice source for a local newsletter. Include support, the main objection, the evidence limitation, and the next step. Then label each sentence as a source finding, a source limitation, or a recommendation. Remove your own unsupported opinion. Check the denominator whenever you use a proportion: ninety supporters out of 150 respondents does not mean ninety percent.
examples: Sixty percent of respondents supported the lane.
The report recommends adding traffic data before a decision.

questions.prompt: Which sentence preserves the source’s distinction between expectation and measurement?
options: The bus lane definitely reduced journey times.
Respondents expected more reliable journeys; journey times were not measured.
Traffic data proved every objection false.
questions.explanation: It reports the expectation while explicitly retaining the absence of direct measurements.

questions.prompt: Ninety supporters out of 150 respondents equals…
questions.explanation: 90 divided by 150 is 0.6, or 60%; the group is respondents, not all residents.

questions.prompt: Which summary conclusion matches the report?
options: The bus lane must be rejected immediately.
The survey alone proves the lane works.
Feedback should be combined with traffic data before a final decision.
questions.explanation: The source recommends combining opinion feedback with traffic measurements before deciding.

lessons.title: Make key words easy to hear
lessons.description: Use word stress, sentence stress, and helpful pauses.

content.heading: Notice the strong syllable
content.text: A stressed syllable is usually more prominent than nearby syllables. Learning the stress as part of a new word can improve recognition as well as speaking. For example, the noun PHOtograph and the noun phoTOGraphy have different stress patterns. Capital letters here show teaching emphasis, not normal spelling. Listen, repeat, and keep all the other syllables audible without giving them equal force.
examples: PHOtograph → phoTOGraphy
TAble → aBOUT

content.heading: Highlight the message
content.text: In a neutral sentence, important nouns, main verbs, and descriptive words often carry prominence. Small grammar words are often less prominent, but they become strong when you need a contrast. Pause at a meaning boundary instead of separating every word. Aim for an understandable rhythm that helps your listener follow the idea rather than copying one particular accent.
examples: I need the BLUE folder, please.
We can meet after lunch / if the room is free.

content.heading: Record and compare
content.text: Prepare a thirty-second introduction to a hobby or useful skill. Mark three important words and two natural pause points before speaking. Record it if possible, then listen for whether the key information stands out. Repeat with one improvement at a time. Keep your voice comfortable: prominence comes from a combination of pitch, duration, and clarity, not simply shouting.
examples: I started gardening / because I wanted to grow herbs.
The most useful tool / is a SMALL watering can.

questions.prompt: In a neutral request for a blue folder, which word is useful to emphasize when colour matters?
options: The word the in every situation
questions.explanation: Blue identifies the distinguishing information, so prominence helps the listener choose the right folder.

questions.prompt: Where is a helpful pause in this sentence?
options: We can meet after lunch / if the room is free.
We can meet after / lunch if the / room is free.
We can meet after lunch if the room / is / free.
questions.explanation: The pause separates the main proposal from its condition at a natural meaning boundary.

questions.prompt: What is the best goal of this practice?
options: Make key information clear at a comfortable pace
Use only one permitted English accent
questions.explanation: Stress and pausing serve intelligibility; there is no single required accent.

lessons.title: Connect words without losing clarity
lessons.description: Practise consonant-to-vowel links and ask for precise repetition.

content.heading: Hear words inside a stream
content.text: In connected speech, words are not always separated by silence. A final consonant can link smoothly to a following vowel, as in pick it up or turn off. The words remain separate grammatical units even when they sound connected. Practise slowly first, then at a natural comfortable speed, keeping the key consonants clear rather than forcing a fast performance.
examples: pick it up → practise as one short group
turn off the light → link turn and off

content.heading: Recognize common weaker forms
content.text: Small words such as to, a, and and often have weaker pronunciations in ordinary speech. Their exact sound varies by accent and context, and speakers can use a strong form for contrast. Learn to recognize these patterns while listening, but do not deliberately swallow words you cannot yet say clearly. Clarity and understanding are more important than maximum speed.
examples: I want to ask a question.
Tea and coffee are available.

content.heading: Repair the exact missing piece
content.text: When a linked phrase is unclear, ask about the part you missed rather than repeatedly requesting the whole message. Practise a dialogue giving an address, collection time, and object. Your partner should ask one focused question, and you should repeat that detail in a clear word group. Check comprehension by having your partner summarize the final arrangement.
examples: Did you say pick it up at eight?
Could you repeat the street name, please?

questions.prompt: Which phrase contains a useful final-consonant-to-vowel link?
questions.explanation: The final consonants of pick and it can link to the following vowel sounds.

questions.prompt: You heard a collection instruction but missed the time. What is the most focused repair?
options: Could you repeat the collection time, please?
Please repeat every conversation this week.
questions.explanation: A focused request identifies the exact information that needs clarification.

questions.prompt: When practising connected speech, you should…
options: speak as fast as possible regardless of clarity.
keep words understandable and increase speed gradually.
assume every accent uses identical weak forms.
questions.explanation: Connected speech should support natural intelligibility, and patterns vary across speakers.

lessons.title: Agree on a plan together
lessons.description: Propose, give a reason, offer an alternative, and confirm.

content.heading: Offer a specific proposal
content.text: A useful proposal includes an activity, time, and place when they matter. Invite the other person’s view instead of assuming agreement. If you cannot accept a suggestion, give a brief reason and offer an alternative. This keeps the conversation moving toward a workable arrangement rather than ending with a simple refusal.
examples: Shall we practise at the library on Thursday at six?
I work until six. Could we meet at seven instead?

content.heading: Explore a workable compromise
content.text: Listen for the underlying need: time, price, travel, or quiet space. Two people may disagree about the first suggestion but share a goal. Use questions to find which details can change. A compromise should address both people’s constraints, not just replace one suggestion with an unrelated idea that leaves the original problem unsolved.
examples: Would an online call save you the bus journey?
If the library closes early, we could use the community room.

content.heading: Role-play and confirm
content.text: Role-play planning a study session. Person A needs a quiet place and cannot travel far; person B is available only after work. Make two proposals, explain one difficulty each, and agree on an alternative. End by repeating the final time, place, and preparation. Your partner should correct any mismatch before the conversation closes.
examples: So, Thursday at seven in the community room.
I will bring the reading exercises; can you bring a notebook?

questions.prompt: Which response keeps negotiation moving?
options: I cannot come at six; would seven work instead?
questions.explanation: It gives a clear constraint and offers a specific alternative.

questions.prompt: One person needs quiet, and the other cannot travel far. What question explores both needs?
options: Why do you dislike every place?
How many words are in quiet?
Is there a quiet room near your home?
questions.explanation: The question searches for a location that meets the quiet-space and travel constraints.

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of a final confirmation?
options: To check that both people share the same final arrangement
To introduce a completely new topic
To avoid naming the place or time
questions.explanation: Repeating the final details catches mismatches before the plan is acted on.

lessons.title: Present a proposal in two minutes
lessons.description: Organize a claim, support, limitation, and audience question.

content.heading: Give the listener a route
content.text: A short presentation needs a clear purpose and a manageable structure. Open with the problem and your proposed response, then tell the audience which two points you will explain. Signposts help when they reveal actual relationships between ideas. Avoid spending half your available time announcing a long agenda instead of developing the proposal itself.
examples: I propose a weekly repair session for residents.
I will explain the need, then outline a small trial.

content.heading: Support and qualify the proposal
content.text: Explain how your idea would address the problem, using a specific illustration or verified evidence. Acknowledge the most important practical limitation and show how a trial could test it. Do not invent statistics to make the presentation sound authoritative. A clear conditional statement is often more useful than an unsupported promise that the proposal will solve every difficulty.
examples: A monthly trial would show whether enough volunteers are available.
If demand exceeds capacity, bookings could limit waiting.

content.heading: Practise delivery and questions
content.text: Prepare a two-minute proposal for a study club, repair session, or community event. Use brief notes with one main idea per line. Mark pauses after the problem, the supporting reason, and the final recommendation. Finish with a direct question inviting the kind of feedback you need, then practise answering a concern by acknowledging it and explaining a relevant adjustment.
examples: Which evening would make this accessible to the most residents?
That capacity concern is useful; we could begin with ten bookings.

questions.prompt: Which opening most clearly states a purpose?
options: There are many things and this is a presentation.
I propose a four-week trial of a community study club.
Before anything, here are twenty unrelated definitions.
questions.explanation: The opening names a concrete proposal and a scope for testing it.

questions.prompt: Which response handles a concern constructively?
options: Every concern is wrong by definition.
There can never be any limitation.
That concern is useful; a booking limit could help us test capacity.
I will repeat my title instead of answering.
questions.explanation: It acknowledges the relevant concern and offers a specific way to address it.

questions.prompt: What should brief presentation notes mainly contain?
options: An entire essay to read without looking up
Every possible fact about the topic
Main ideas and cues that support the structure
questions.explanation: Brief idea cues help you maintain a logical route while speaking to the audience.

lessons.title: Negotiate a fair practical trade-off
lessons.description: Separate positions from needs and make conditional offers.

content.heading: Find the need behind the position
content.text: A position is what someone initially asks for; an underlying need explains why it matters. A team asking for a Friday deadline may need time for review, while another asking for Wednesday may need to reserve equipment. Ask an open clarification question before defending your first proposal. Understanding the reason can reveal an option both sides had missed.
examples: What needs to happen before your team can approve it?
Is the main constraint the review time or the printing slot?

content.heading: Offer a conditional exchange
content.text: Use if, provided that, or as long as to connect a concession with a necessary condition. State what you can offer and what must happen in return. Check that a conditional offer is not being heard as unconditional agreement. Keep the action, owner, and timing explicit so the compromise can be evaluated rather than remaining a polite but vague intention.
examples: We can send the draft on Wednesday if feedback arrives by Thursday noon.
I can reduce the order provided that delivery remains on Monday.

content.heading: Role-play and close clearly
content.text: Negotiate an event plan with a partner: one person needs a low cost, and the other needs a reliable indoor space. Identify the needs, exchange two options, and make one conditional offer. Finish with a short spoken summary of responsibilities and unresolved items. Invite a correction so both sides can distinguish a firm agreement from a detail still awaiting confirmation.
examples: Agreed: use the smaller hall; I will check availability today.
The price is still provisional until the venue confirms.

questions.prompt: Which question explores the reason behind a deadline request?
options: What review steps must you complete before approval?
Will you agree without any information?
questions.explanation: The question investigates the underlying process rather than attacking the stated position.

questions.prompt: We can deliver Friday provided that approval arrives Wednesday means…
options: Friday delivery depends on Wednesday approval.
Friday delivery is guaranteed regardless of approval.
No delivery is possible under any condition.
questions.explanation: Provided that introduces the condition required for the offer to apply.

questions.prompt: What should a closing negotiation summary distinguish?
options: Personal preferences unrelated to the task
Agreed actions and details still awaiting confirmation
questions.explanation: A useful summary records commitments while keeping unresolved items visible.

lessons.title: Use emphasis to show the intended contrast
lessons.description: Control prominent words, thought groups, and careful clarification.

content.heading: Move prominence to change the contrast
content.text: Sentence prominence can show which part of a message corrects an assumption. Compare I ordered the BLUE folder with I ORDERED the blue folder. The first contrasts colours; the second can contrast ordering with receiving or borrowing. Context is essential: prominence suggests the focus, while the surrounding exchange helps the listener interpret the exact contrast.
examples: I said MONDAY, not Tuesday.
MAYA sent the file, not Leon.

content.heading: Group complex ideas for the listener
content.text: Divide a longer turn into thought groups, with each group carrying one useful step in the reasoning. Pause before a qualification or a contrasting point when that helps comprehension. Avoid treating every comma as an obligatory long silence. Test your delivery by asking a partner to summarize the main claim and the limitation after one listen.
examples: The trial reduced waiting / but only during quieter mornings.
If the room is available / we can move the workshop indoors.

content.heading: Clarify without implying blame
content.text: Practise correcting a misunderstanding about a booking time, a project result, or a responsibility. Emphasize the corrected detail and state it plainly. A neutral phrase such as to clarify can reduce tension, but tone and the whole message matter. Record two versions and check whether the second is both clear and respectful rather than merely louder or more forceful.
examples: To clarify, the figure refers to VISITS, not individual visitors.
I meant the draft is ready for REVIEW, not publication.

questions.prompt: To correct Tuesday to Monday, which word should receive the key prominence?
questions.explanation: Prominence on Monday highlights the corrected day.

questions.prompt: The trial reduced waiting, but only during quieter mornings. Which summary preserves the limitation?
options: Waiting fell during quieter mornings; other periods are not established.
The trial proved mornings are always quiet.
Waiting was never measured in any form.
questions.explanation: The summary retains the restricted time context rather than extending the result.

questions.prompt: Which clarification is precise and respectful?
options: You clearly understand nothing at all.
To clarify, the count refers to visits, not different visitors.
I will shout the same unclear number.
Everyone should guess what I meant.
questions.explanation: The sentence corrects the specific distinction without assigning blame to the listener.

words.meaning: An arrangement to meet someone at a particular time.
words.example: I made an appointment with the course adviser.

words.meaning: The physical or mental energy used to do something.
words.example: She made an effort to learn every classmate’s name.

words.meaning: To arrange for an event to happen at a later time.
words.example: We postponed the picnic because heavy rain was forecast.

words.meaning: Able to be trusted to work well or behave as expected.
words.example: A reliable bus service helps people arrive on time.

words.meaning: A change that makes something better.
words.example: There was a clear improvement in the organization of his essay.

words.meaning: A person who offers to do something without being forced and often without payment.
words.example: A volunteer checked the community fridge each morning.

words.meaning: A person or thing that takes the place of another.
words.example: The shop sent a replacement for the damaged chair.

words.meaning: Money returned to someone after a purchase or payment.
words.example: I requested a refund because the class was cancelled.

words.meaning: Agreement that allows someone to do something.
words.example: Please ask permission before recording the discussion.

words.meaning: To state that an arrangement or piece of information is correct or definite.
words.example: Could you confirm the meeting time by email?

words.meaning: To make a damaged or broken thing work properly again.
words.example: The volunteer helped repair my lamp.

words.meaning: An agreed responsibility or promise to give time or effort.
words.example: The reading role requires a ten-week commitment.

words.meaning: The ability or opportunity to enter a place or use something.
words.example: The plumber needs access to the pipes under the sink.

words.meaning: A small piece of writing that identifies or describes something.
words.example: Write the preparation date on the food label.

words.meaning: Another possible choice or course of action.
words.example: An online meeting is an alternative to travelling across town.

words.meaning: Correct in its details and free from important errors.
words.example: Check that your order number is accurate before sending the email.

words.meaning: A limit or condition that restricts what can be done.
words.example: The last bus home was the main constraint on her course choice.

words.meaning: An agreement in which people adjust their demands to reach a workable result.
words.example: They reached a compromise by using a smaller hall for less money.

words.meaning: Included in smaller numbers than would fairly reflect a wider group.
words.example: People without internet access may be underrepresented in the online survey.

words.meaning: To regard something as having a particular cause or source.
words.example: We cannot attribute the change to the course without considering other explanations.

words.meaning: The freedom to decide what should be done in a particular situation.
words.example: The manager has discretion to accept a late booking.

words.meaning: Able to be paid back under stated conditions.
words.example: The deposit is refundable if the room is left clean.

words.meaning: Fair and not favouring one person or side.
words.example: An impartial reviewer considers the strengths of both proposals.

words.meaning: Something accepted or given up to help reach an agreement.
words.example: Offering a later deadline was an important concession in the negotiation.

words.meaning: The process of putting a plan or decision into effect.
words.example: The report recommends another trial before full implementation.

words.meaning: Relating to whether one thing produces an effect on another.
words.example: The survey does not establish a causal link between the policy and the result.

words.meaning: Looking back at or describing past events.
words.example: The questionnaire relied on retrospective accounts of last year’s working conditions.

words.meaning: The way someone notices, understands, or experiences something.
words.example: The report measured staff perceptions rather than task performance.

words.meaning: An action that corrects or improves an undesirable situation.
words.example: A replacement part may be an appropriate remedy for the fault.

words.meaning: A difference between things that are expected to match.
words.example: There is a discrepancy between the invoice total and the amount charged.

words.meaning: Depending on a particular requirement or situation.
words.example: Their agreement is conditional on approval of the final map.

words.meaning: The range of matters or situations included in something.
words.example: Keep your conclusion within the scope of the evidence.
